derivations.claim: Let $T:V_N\to\mathbb C^N$ be given by $T(p)=(p^{(k)}(\lambda_i))_{i,k}$. By [F2], $T$ is linear, and by [F1] its domain and codomain both have dimension $N$.

If $N=0$, then $V_N=\{0\}$, so $T$ is injective. If $N>0$ and $T(p)=0$, the exact Taylor expansion of the polynomial at $\lambda_i$ shows $(z-\lambda_i)^{m_i}$ divides $p$ for every $i$. The factors for distinct $\lambda_i$ are pairwise coprime, so their product of degree $N$ divides $p$. Since $p\in V_N$ has degree less than $N$, this forces $p=0$. Thus $T$ is injective in either case.
An injective linear map between finite-dimensional spaces of the same dimension is surjective, so the prescribed vector $(c_{i,k})_{i,k}$ has a preimage under $T$ and that preimage is unique.

For an integer $m\ge0$, put
$$a_{m,j}:=\frac{(2m-j)!\,m!}{(2m)!\,j!\,(m-j)!}\qquad(0\le j\le m), \qquad p_m(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m a_{m,j}z^j, \qquad q_m(z):=p_m(-z).$$
The diagonal Padé rational function of order $m$ for the scalar exponential
[[def-complex-exponential]] is
$$r_m(z):=\frac{p_m(z)}{q_m(z)}$$
at every $z\in\mathbb C$ for which $q_m(z)\ne0$. The pair is normalized by
$p_m(0)=q_m(0)=1$. This definition does not assign a value at a zero of the
denominator.

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

derivations.claim: Set $g_m(t)=t^m(1-t)^m$. For $z\ne0$, integration by parts $2m+1$ times, using $g_m^{(2m+1)}=0$, gives $\int_0^1 e^{tz}g_m(t)\,dt= \left[e^{tz}\sum_{k=0}^{2m}\frac{(-1)^k g_m^{(k)}(t)}{z^{k+1}}\right]_{t=0}^{t=1}.$ For $k<m$, both endpoint derivatives vanish. For $k=m+\ell$ with $0\le\ell\le m$, expansion of $t^m(1-t)^m$ at the endpoints gives $g_m^{(k)}(1)=(-1)^m\binom m\ell(m+\ell)!$ and $g_m^{(k)}(0)=(-1)^\ell\binom m\ell(m+\ell)!$. After multiplication by $(-1)^m z^{2m+1}/(2m)!$, the coefficient of $e^z z^{m-\ell}$ is $(-1)^{m-\ell}\binom m\ell(m+\ell)!/(2m)!=(-1)^{m-\ell}a_{m,m-\ell}$, and the coefficient of $z^{m-\ell}$ without $e^z$ is $-\binom m\ell(m+\ell)!/(2m)!=-a_{m,m-\ell}$. These are exactly the coefficients of $q_m(z)e^z-p_m(z)$, so collecting the powers gives $q_m(z)e^z-p_m(z)=\frac{(-1)^m z^{2m+1}}{(2m)!} \int_0^1 e^{tz}t^m(1-t)^m\,dt.$ Both sides are continuous at $z=0$, so the identity holds there as well.

By the triangle inequality, $|q_m(z)|=|p_m(-z)|\ge1-\sum_{j=1}^m a_{m,j}|z|^j\ge d_m(\rho)>0$. Thus $q_m$ has no zero in the disk. Also $\int_0^1t^m(1-t)^m\,dt=\frac{(m!)^2}{(2m+1)!},$ as follows by integrating by parts $m$ times and then integrating $(1-t)^{2m}$. Hence $\left|\int_0^1e^{tz}t^m(1-t)^m\,dt\right| \le e^\rho(m!)^2/(2m+1)!$.
Divide the identity in step 1.1 by the nonzero $q_m(z)$ from step 2.1 and use $|z|^{2m+1}\le\rho^{2m+1}$. This gives the stated remainder bound.

Let $s\ge0$, let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s\in\mathbb C$ be distinct, let
$m_1,\ldots,m_s$ be positive integers, and put $N=\sum_{i=1}^s m_i$. Let
$V_N=\operatorname{span}\{1,z,\ldots,z^{N-1}\}$, with the empty span
$V_0=\{0\}$. For arbitrary data
$c_{i,k}\in\mathbb C$ with $1\le i\le s$ and $0\le k<m_i$, there is exactly
one polynomial $p\in V_N$ satisfying
$$p^{(k)}(\lambda_i)=c_{i,k}\qquad(1\le i\le s,\ 0\le k<m_i).$$

An endomorphism of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space has a Jordan canonical form over $F$ if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $F$. This includes the zero space, where the characteristic polynomial is $1$ and the Jordan form is empty.

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]], [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]].

Let $A,B\in M_n(F)$ have characteristic polynomials that split over $F$. Then $A$ and $B$ are similar if and only if their Jordan canonical forms have the same multiset of Jordan blocks. The blocks may occur in different orders.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic,
and let $\Gamma$ be a complex chain which is a cycle, with trace in $\Omega$ and
null-homologous in $\Omega$. Then for every natural number $m$ and every
$z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$

$$n(\Gamma,z)\,f^{(m)}(z)=\frac{m!}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z)^{m+1}}\,d\zeta,$$

with $f^{(0)}=f$. The case $m=0$ is the integral formula already proved.

Let $\Gamma=\sum_{k<r}m_k\gamma_k$ be a complex chain
([[def-complex-chain-and-cycle]]) with trace $\Gamma^\ast$, and let $f$ be
continuous on $\Gamma^\ast$. The **integral of $f$ over $\Gamma$** is

$$\int_\Gamma f(z)\,dz:=\sum_{\substack{k<r\\ m_k\ne0}}m_k\int_{\gamma_k}f(z)\,dz,$$

a finite sum ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]) of the complex line
integrals of [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]]. Each summand
exists: for $k$ with $m_k\ne0$ the trace $\gamma_k^\ast$ is contained in
$\Gamma^\ast$, so $f$ is continuous on it, and $\gamma_k$ is rectifiable, so
[[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]] applies. Terms
with $m_k=0$ are omitted, so no integral of $f$ over a contour outside the trace
is required. The empty chain, and any chain all of whose coefficients vanish,
give $\int_\Gamma f\,dz=0$.

For $p\in\mathbb C\setminus\Gamma^\ast$, the **index of $\Gamma$ about $p$** is

$$n(\Gamma,p):=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma\frac{dz}{z-p}.$$

This is defined: $z\mapsto 1/(z-p)$ is complex differentiable, hence continuous,
on $\mathbb C\setminus\{p\}\supseteq\Gamma^\ast$ by
[[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be normal. If $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$,
then there are pairwise orthogonal projections $P_1,\dots,P_r$ such that

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

each $P_j$ projects onto the eigenspace $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$, and every $P_j$ is
a polynomial in $T$.

derivations.claim: Let $C$ be any finite complex square matrix whose eigenvalues lie in $\Omega$, let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s$ be its distinct eigenvalues, and let $m_i$ be the largest Jordan-block size at $\lambda_i$. By [F2], there is a unique polynomial $p$ of degree less than $\sum_i m_i$ with $p^{(k)}(\lambda_i)=f^{(k)}(\lambda_i)$ for $k<m_i$.

On a block $J_d(\lambda)=\lambda I+N$, the finite geometric identity $(zI-J_d(\lambda))^{-1} =\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\frac{N^k}{(z-\lambda)^{k+1}}$ holds whenever $z\ne\lambda$, since multiplication by $(z-\lambda)I-N$ cancels adjacent terms and $N^d=0$.

For every integer $k\ge0$, the higher product rule is $(fg)^{(k)}=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}f^{(j)}g^{(k-j)}$: the case $k=0$ is the product itself; differentiate the finite sum using [F6] and combine adjacent terms by $\binom{k}{j-1}+\binom{k}{j}=\binom{k+1}{j}$ to obtain the successor case. Thus on each Jordan block, multiplying the finite Taylor jets has degree-$k$ coefficient $\sum_{j=0}^k f^{(j)}(\lambda)g^{(k-j)}(\lambda)/(j!(k-j)!)=(fg)^{(k)}(\lambda)/k!$. Since $N_d^d=0$, terms of degree at least $d$ vanish, and the resulting block is exactly the jet of $fg$. Conjugating block by block proves $(fg)(A)=f(A)g(A)$.

For each Jordan block $J_d(\lambda_i)=\lambda_iI+N_d$, the exact finite Taylor expansion of $p$ at $\lambda_i$ gives $p(J_d(\lambda_i))=\sum_{k<d}p^{(k)}(\lambda_i)N_d^k/k!$ because $N_d^d=0$. Since $d\le m_i$, these derivatives equal those of $f$; hence $p(C)$ equals the Jordan expression in [F1].

Apply [F4] to each eigenvalue $\lambda$ with index one. Integrating the finite sum in step 1.2 term by term therefore gives $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f(z)(zI-J_d(\lambda))^{-1}\,dz =\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(\lambda)}{k!}N^k.$ The integral is a finite sum of scalar integrals, so entrywise linearity justifies the operation.

By [F3], any other Jordan representation has the same block multiset, so the same nodes and maximal sizes determine the same unique polynomial $p$. Thus its Jordan expression is again $p(C)$. For invertible $X$, $(XCX^{-1})^k=XC^kX^{-1}$ for every $k$, so $p(XCX^{-1})=Xp(C)X^{-1}$. This proves independence and similarity invariance for every $C$.

Let $T$ be block upper triangular and let $p$ be the Hermite polynomial obtained by applying steps 1.1–1.2 with $C=T$. Every power of $T$ is block upper triangular, with $i$th diagonal block $T_{ii}^k$; hence $p(T)$ has diagonal blocks $p(T_{ii})$. If a polynomial annihilates $T$, its diagonal blocks show that it also annihilates every $T_{ii}$, so the minimal polynomial of each $T_{ii}$ divides that of $T$. Therefore the Jordan block sizes required for $T_{ii}$ are no larger than those used for $T$, and the Hermite conditions give $p(T_{ii})=f(T_{ii})$. Since $f(T)=p(T)$ by steps 1.1–1.2 applied to $T$, the claimed block structure and diagonal blocks follow.

Conjugating the blockwise identity in step 2.2 by the Jordan basis matrix $Z$ and using the definition in [F1] proves the contour formula. If $A$ is normal, [F5] supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis and all Jordan blocks have size one; the same formula is $\sum_\lambda f(\lambda)P_\lambda$, which is the stated spectral functional calculus.

derivations.claim: On a Jordan block $J=\lambda I+N$ of size $d$, the primary value of a holomorphic $h$ is $\sum_{k<d}h^{(k)}(\lambda)N^k/k!$. Products of such truncated Taylor polynomials agree modulo $N^d$ with the truncated Taylor polynomial of the scalar product, by the finite Leibniz rule. For composition, write the inner Taylor series as $\lambda+\sum_{j\ge1}a_j u^j$ modulo $u^d$; substitution into the outer Taylor polynomial and discarding powers $u^d$ and higher gives exactly the Taylor series of the scalar composition modulo $u^d$. Thus analytic identities on a neighborhood of $\lambda$ remain valid on this Jordan block. In particular, the matrix exponential series agrees with the primary value of the scalar exponential: the binomial theorem and absolute convergence in [F5] give $\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{J^n}{n!} =\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\frac{N^k}{k!} \left(\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{\lambda^r}{r!}\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\frac{e^\lambda N^k}{k!}.$ Only finitely many nilpotent powers occur, so rearranging the absolutely convergent sum is legitimate.

Applying step 1.1 to $\exp\circ\operatorname{Log}(z)=z$ and $(z^{1/2}_{\operatorname{Log}})^2=z$ gives $\exp(L(A))=A$ and $R(A)^2=A$ block by block and then by similarity. The eigenvalues of these primary matrices are their scalar values at the eigenvalues of $A$, so [F1] and [F2] give the stated strip and right-half-plane restrictions.

Suppose $Y$ is another logarithm of $A$ with spectrum in the open strip. On a Jordan block at $\mu\in\sigma(Y)$, $\exp(\mu)$ lies in $S$ and $\operatorname{Log}(\exp z)=z$ on a neighborhood of $\mu$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $\operatorname{Log}(\exp(J))=J$. Applying this on every block of $Y$ and using similarity invariance yields $L(A)=\operatorname{Log}(\exp(Y))=Y$.

Suppose $Q^2=A$ and $\sigma(Q)$ lies in the open right half-plane. Put $D=Q-R(A)$. Then $QD+DR(A)=Q(Q-R(A))+(Q-R(A))R(A)=Q^2-R(A)^2=0$. The spectra of $Q$ and $R(A)$ lie in the right half-plane, so $\sigma(Q)\cap(-\sigma(R(A)))=\varnothing$. By [F4], the homogeneous Sylvester equation has only the zero solution; hence $D=0$ and $Q=R(A)$.

derivations.claim: For compatible matrices $U,V$, Cauchy–Schwarz applied to each entry gives $|(UV)_{ij}|^2\le(\sum_k|u_{ik}|^2)(\sum_k|v_{kj}|^2)$. Summing over $i,j$ proves $\|UV\|_F\le\|U\|_F\|V\|_F$. Use this submultiplicative Frobenius norm below.

The cycle trace is compact and disjoint from $\sigma(A)$, so $R(z)=(zI-A)^{-1}$ is continuous and bounded on it. By [F4], each eigenvalue of $A$ has an open neighborhood contained in $\Omega$ and disjoint from the trace on which the cycle index remains one (intersect the index neighborhood with $\Omega$, which is open and contains that eigenvalue); the finite union of these neighborhoods is an open index-one region $U_1$. Every sufficiently small $H$ has $\sigma(A+H)\subset U_1$: otherwise choose $H_j\to0$ and $\lambda_j\in\sigma(A+H_j)\setminus U_1$. Normalize corresponding eigenvectors to Euclidean norm one; Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\lambda_j|\le\|A+H_j\|_F$, so a subsequence converges to some $\lambda$. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, define
$$
\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\sum_{j=1}^n |a_{ij}|.
$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$, define $\|x\|_\infty:=\max_j|x_j|$. The absolute value is the complex modulus $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$. The subscript on the matrix norm emphasizes that entries and vectors are complex; this definition is not an appeal to the real-only induced matrix p-norm convention. For square matrices the identity has norm $1$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: Endpoint matching makes the two expressions agree at $1/2$, so this formula defines a map even when the factors are not paths. If both factors are complex contours, their continuity and endpoint matching make the concatenation continuous, including at the join. In this case the concatenation is rectifiable and its length is $L_{\mathbb C}(\alpha)+L_{\mathbb C}(\beta)$: inserting $1/2$ into a partition can only increase its sum by the triangle inequality; the refined sum splits into two sums of the factors, while combining partitions from both factors gives the reverse supremum inequality. Taking factor sums within $\varepsilon/2$ of their finite suprema proves equality. This argument includes constant pieces. Reversal preserves rectifiability and length by [[thm-complex-path-length-invariant-under-monotone-reparametrization]].

Input exact complex matrices $M\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $C\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$, $n,r\ge1$, and a nonnegative integer candidate-operation budget $K$. Retain their exact real/imaginary values for the final audit. Rational complex inputs $M,C\in\mathbb Q(i)$ are included.

The verification/controller model is an exact real-RAM: its scalar field operations $+,-,\times,/$, zero/order comparisons, finite indices and copies act on the exact input/stored real values. Complex controller operations mean their real-component field formulas. The final audit uses the fixed row-major loops for $M\widehat X-C$, with inner products summed in increasing index order, and tests all real/imaginary components for zero. These are prescribed finite expression trees/loops, not an unprovided certification oracle. No implementation or bit-cost claim for arbitrary real encodings is made. In a rational adapter, exact rational inputs and a supplied finite format codebook give every stored real code its exact rational value; decoding is finite table lookup. When all required codes/values are supplied, the same audit is finite exact rational arithmetic (binary formats give dyadic values). Missing/invalid adapter data return `representation-inconclusive`; they are not silently assumed. The default exact real-RAM route requires no rational/dyadic decoder.

Candidate operations use
[[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Charge one budget unit BEFORE each rounded real primitive, including each component conversion and every primitive inside a called norm, reflector, complex product, subtraction or division. On exhaustion return `budget-exhausted` with any available partial candidate. Successful exact controller operations, index loops, comparisons, conjugations and copies are separate from this rounded-operation budget; their loops are finite and no total cubic or bit-cost assertion is made here. Each excluded rounded intermediate returns `range-failure` with its index and partial values. Required stored scalar constants must be admissible, or the candidate route returns `candidate-failure`.

**Instrumented kernel execution.** The calls in steps2–3 are macros, not opaque subroutine calls: expand the actual finite loops and scalar expressions of the two named Householder definitions, including the scaled real-component norm, phase-modulus norm, stored-vector squared norm, all sequential real dot operations, real-scalar component multiplication, six-real-operation complex products, additions/subtractions, divisions and square roots. Replace each requested rounded real primitive or component conversion by the following dispatcher. With counter $b$ initially zero, first test $b=K$; if equal, return `budget-exhausted` immediately without evaluating that primitive. Otherwise increase $b$ by one and execute exactly that one primitive in the source arithmetic model; propagate its first failure. No macro, norm or reflector is executed before its primitives are dispatched, and no budget count is guessed after a completed call. Keep all source loop indices, zero branches, target overwrites, success/failure labels and operation order; a zero-column marker represents the identity and skips reflector denominators and RHS arithmetic. Exact control comparisons/copies remain separate. This is a budgeted execution of the same kernels, not a replacement numerical method. A fully funded execution is identical to the source operation trace. A partial candidate includes an explicit completed-entry mask and is never presented as a complete solution matrix. The exact audit in step4 is reached only after every one of the $nr$ solution entries is successfully computed.

1. Round each real/imaginary component of $M,C$ to form stored candidates $R,D$. A failed conversion returns `range-failure` (or `budget-exhausted` before an unaffordable conversion).
2. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, call
[[alg-complex-scaled-householder-reflector-step]] with target $R_{k:n,k}$ and trailing block $R_{k:n,k+1:n}$. Retain its target overwrite and trailing update, and store $v,\widehat\tau$ and the represented factor. Propagate `breakdown`, `range-failure` and budget exhaustion. A zero-column identity branch copies the blocks. Replay this SAME stored reflector on the active RHS panel $D_{k:n,:}$ in formation order, without any target overwrite, using the separate-block kernel of
[[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]]: for each RHS column $j$ compute
$$d_j=\operatorname{fl}\!\left(\sum_{i=k}^n\overline v_iD_{ij}\right),\quad p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i),\quad z_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(p_id_j),\quad D_{ij}\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(D_{ij}-z_{ij}).$$
Use increasing indices, sequential dots, componentwise real-coefficient multiplication and the declared complex products; reuse $p_i$ if already stored. Identity reflectors copy $D$. Do not feed nonstored normalized reflector entries to floating operations. After the column step, if $R_{kk}=0$, return `zero-pivot`.
3. For each RHS $j$ in increasing order and each row $i=n,\ldots,1$, start $s=D_{ij}$ and for $\ell=i+1,\ldots,n$ set $s\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(s-\operatorname{fl}(R_{i\ell}\widehat X_{\ell j}))$. This is the rounded backward recurrence of
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]. To divide $s=a+ib$ by the nonzero stored pivot $R_{ii}=c+id$, use ONLY the following rounded real primitives in the displayed order:
$$t=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(c c)+\operatorname{fl}(d d)),\quad p=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(a c)+\operatorname{fl}(b d)),\quad q=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(b c)-\operatorname{fl}(a d)),$$
$$\widehat X_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(p/t)+i\operatorname{fl}(q/t).$$
Reject $t\le0$ as `range-failure`; every other nonzero excluded intermediate also fails under the scalar model. This deliberately conservative routine can fail on range even for a nonzero pivot; it is not a new complex-division primitive. Other invalid candidate data return `candidate-failure`.
4. Compute $M\widehat X-C$ in the declared exact controller on the original inputs and exact stored values. If it is exactly zero, return `verified-solution` with $\widehat X$; otherwise return `candidate-unverified` with $\widehat X$ and the exact nonzero residual. Use the rational adapter only when its actual encoded-data preconditions hold.

Every candidate loop has finite dimensions and budget; every exact audit loop has a fixed finite index set. No accuracy, stability or uniqueness is inferred from the candidate generation. A verified solution need not be unique unless the caller separately knows $M$ invertible. All original rational-input/decoded-format instances remain available through the explicit adapter.

For an integer $m\ge0$, put
$$a_{m,j}:=\frac{(2m-j)!\,m!}{(2m)!\,j!\,(m-j)!}\qquad(0\le j\le m), \qquad p_m(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m a_{m,j}z^j, \qquad q_m(z):=p_m(-z).$$
The diagonal Padé rational function of order $m$ for the scalar exponential
[[def-complex-exponential]] is
$$r_m(z):=\frac{p_m(z)}{q_m(z)}$$
at every $z\in\mathbb C$ for which $q_m(z)\ne0$. The pair is normalized by
$p_m(0)=q_m(0)=1$. This definition does not assign a value at a zero of the
denominator.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the exact residual $MX-C$ is zero, so the returned matrix satisfies $MX=C$.

If $M$ is invertible, left multiplication by $M^{-1}$ gives $X=M^{-1}C$, which is the unique solution. In the Padé use, take $M=Q_m(B)=q_m(B)$ and $C=P_m(B)=p_m(B)$ by [F2]; the conclusion applies whenever this denominator matrix is invertible.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $f$ be holomorphic on an open
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ containing $\sigma(A)$, and let $r$ be rational
with no pole on $\Omega$. Let $\Gamma$ be an admissible Cauchy cycle for $A$
contained in $\Omega$, with total contour length $L_\Gamma$. Suppose
$$\sup_{z\in\Gamma}|f(z)-r(z)|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \sup_{z\in\Gamma}\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le M.$$
Then
$$\|f(A)-r(A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le \frac{L_\Gamma}{2\pi}\,\varepsilon M.$$
The resolvent hypothesis may be supplied by the diskwise certificate of
[[thm-complex-resolvent-cover-certificate-soundness]]. A scalar disk error
alone does not give this matrix bound for a nonnormal matrix.

[[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]], and let

[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]. Choose a Jordan
representation in the convention of [[def-jordan-canonical-form]], which
exists by [[thm-jordan-form-exists-iff-the-characteristic-polynomial-splits]]
and [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra-minimum-modulus-proof]]:
$$A=Z\,\operatorname{diag}(J_{d_1}(\lambda_1),\ldots,J_{d_r}(\lambda_r))\,Z^{-1},$$
where $J_d(\lambda)=\lambda I_d+N_d$ and $N_d$ has ones on its first
superdiagonal and is nilpotent of order at most $d$. Define the Jordan
expression
$$f_J(A):= Z\,\operatorname{diag}\left( \sum_{k=0}^{d_1-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(\lambda_1)}{k!}N_{d_1}^k,\ldots, \sum_{k=0}^{d_r-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(\lambda_r)}{k!}N_{d_r}^k \right)Z^{-1}.$$
The analytic primary matrix function $f(A)$ is this expression, with the same
single scalar branch $f$ and its derivatives used in every block at a repeated
eigenvalue. Its independence of the chosen Jordan representation is discharged
by [[thm-analytic-primary-matrix-function-jordan-contour-agreement]].

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ whose stored entries
are representable in the operationwise model, a Padé order $m\ge0$, an integer
scaling count $s\ge0$, finite nonnegative integer Householder-candidate and squaring-operation budgets,
finite scalar-series budgets, and an
error policy that is either candidate-only or certify. The procedure never
selects adaptive Higham parameters. Certification data, including contour
vertices and the radius, have exact dyadic or rational encodings.

1. Interpret the stored entries of $A$ as their exact real/imaginary values and
   form $B=2^{-s}A$ exactly. Evaluate $P=p_m(B)$ and $Q=q_m(B)$ by exact
   controller matrix arithmetic: increasing-index sums/products and finite
   polynomial powers with their rational coefficients. Use the exact real-RAM
   controller declared in [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]];
   the optional rational adapter is used only when all required actual
   encodings are supplied. No dyadic representation is assumed for the
   abstract floating model.
2. Call [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]] on $QX=P$, explicitly passing the supplied finite Householder-candidate operation budget $K_H$. Continue only if the returned record contains a complete finite stored $n\times n$ matrix, with all entries marked complete, and status `verified-solution` or `candidate-unverified`. A partial candidate or any budget, range, representation or other failure is propagated with its original status and available partial record; do not square it. Retain a complete unverified candidate only in candidate-only mode; certification mode returns denominator-unverified. A complete matrix accompanying a failure status does not authorize continuation.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,s-1$, compute the next matrix square in the operationwise
   model. A range failure returns range-failure with the last candidate.
   Retain their exact stored real values and form
   $D_j=\widehat X_{j+1}-\widehat X_j^2$ by the exact controller's finite
   matrix loops. Set
   $\delta_j=\max_i\sum_k(|\operatorname{Re}(D_j)_{ik}|
   +|\operatorname{Im}(D_j)_{ik}|)$; this exact nonnegative real number bounds
   $\|D_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$.
4. In candidate-only mode, return the final candidate with status
   unevaluated-error-bound. Certification mode has these caller preconditions,
   which the procedure does not itself verify: (a) a supplied polygonal Cauchy
   cycle $\Gamma$ with dyadic vertices, trace in a disk $|z|\le\rho$ for
   dyadic $\rho>0$, $\sigma(B)\subset\{|z|<\rho\}$, disjointness from
   $\sigma(B)$, index one on $\sigma(B)$, and null-homology in that disk;
   (b) $d_m(\rho)>0$; (c) a supplied finite dyadic resolvent-cover input for
   the singleton family $\{B\}$; and (d) a finite term budget $K$.
   The contour-validator call
   [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] must return
   certified-resolvent-cover with bound $M$, or the procedure returns
   inconclusive-resolvent. The validator checks resolvent inequalities and
   segment coverage only; it does not validate the caller's topological
   preconditions or count enclosed eigenvalues. Here $\sigma(B)$ denotes the
   eigenvalue set of $B$ from
   [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]].
5. For $x=\rho$ and for
   $\alpha=\max_i\sum_j(|\operatorname{Re}A_{ij}|+
   |\operatorname{Im}A_{ij}|)$, compute an upper bound $U(x)$ for $e^x$ as
   follows. If $x=0$, set $U(x)=1$. Otherwise, if $x\ge K+2$, return
   inconclusive-scalar-tail. If $x<K+2$, put
   $r=x/(K+2)$,
   $U(x)=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!+
   [x^{K+1}/(K+1)!]/(1-r)$.
   The scalar-tail inequality used by the error theorem is proved separately there; this step defines the finite expression, rather than treating a Definition sentence as its proof.
6. Write the supplied finite polygonal chain as $\Gamma=\sum_\nu m_\nu\gamma_\nu$, with integer coefficients. Let $\ell=\sum_\nu |m_\nu|\sum_{e\text{ in }\gamma_\nu}(|\Delta\operatorname{Re}e|+|\Delta\operatorname{Im}e|)$; then
   $\ell$ is an exact rational upper bound for the coefficient-weighted contour length $L_\Gamma=\sum_\nu|m_\nu|L(\gamma_\nu)$ (the supplied vertices have rational/dyadic encodings). Put
   $\epsilon=\rho^{2m+1}U(\rho)(m!)^2/
   ((2m)!(2m+1)!d_m(\rho))$. Since
   $\pi/4=\int_0^1(1+x^2)^{-1}\,dx$, the finite identity
   $1/(1+x^2)=\sum_{k=0}^7(-1)^kx^{2k}+x^{16}/(1+x^2)$ on $[0,1]$ gives
   $\pi/4>33976/45045>3/4$, hence $1/(2\pi)<1/6$. Set
   $E_0=\ell\epsilon M/6$.
7. For each squaring use
   $E_{j+1}=(2U(\alpha)+E_j)E_j+\delta_j$.
   If every computed certification check succeeded, the denominator solve
   returned verified-solution, and the caller preconditions hold, return the
   final candidate with status conditional-error-bound and bound $E_s$.
   Otherwise retain the candidate and return
   the corresponding inconclusive status.

The exact controller uses only prescribed finite field-expression trees and
loops over dimensions, $m,s$ and the finite scalar-series term budget $K$;
absolute values/maxima use exact comparisons. It performs no additional
unprovided certification call. Count every rounded real primitive of a square
in row-major/increasing inner-index order against an explicitly supplied
finite squaring-operation budget, and propagate `budget-exhausted` before an
unaffordable operation. The solve uses its separately supplied finite
candidate-operation budget. Exact controller work is separate: its values
need not be rational, and no bit-computability or total bit-cost bound for
arbitrary real encodings is claimed. For the optional rational adapter with
all values encoded, these same finite formulas use exact rational arithmetic.
All loops are finite. The conditional-error-bound status is sound
only under the caller preconditions in step 4 and does not mean that the
procedure checked contour topology or eigenvalue count. No floating-point
stability is asserted for the candidate alone.

If [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]] returns
verified-solution with output $X$ for exact complex matrices $M,C$ in its declared exact-controller model, then
$MX=C$ exactly. If $M$ is invertible, this solution is unique; in particular,
when used with an invertible Padé denominator, it is the exact denominator solve. This includes the original rational-input
instance and its finite exact rational audit whenever the adapter encodings
are supplied.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For $m\ge0$ and $\rho\ge0$, put
$$d_m(\rho):=1-\sum_{j=1}^m a_{m,j}\rho^j,$$
with the empty sum equal to zero and $a_{m,j}$ as in
[[def-diagonal-pade-approximant-for-exponential]]. If $d_m(\rho)>0$, then
$q_m$ has no zero in $|z|\le\rho$ and, for every such $z$,
$$\left|e^z-r_m(z)\right| \le \frac{\rho^{2m+1}e^\rho(m!)^2} {(2m)!(2m+1)!\,d_m(\rho)}.$$
This is a finite-order bound; it makes no adaptive choice of $m$ or scaling.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $f$ be holomorphic on an open
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ containing $\sigma(A)$, and let $r$ be rational
with no pole on $\Omega$. Let $\Gamma$ be an admissible Cauchy cycle for $A$
contained in $\Omega$. Write its finite chain representation as $\Gamma=\sum_\nu m_\nu\gamma_\nu$ with integer coefficients and define its coefficient-weighted length by $L_\Gamma:=\sum_\nu|m_\nu|L(\gamma_\nu)$. The integral and this length use the same signed-chain representation. Suppose
$$\sup_{z\in\Gamma}|f(z)-r(z)|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \sup_{z\in\Gamma}\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le M.$$
Then
$$\|f(A)-r(A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le \frac{L_\Gamma}{2\pi}\,\varepsilon M.$$
The resolvent hypothesis may be supplied by the diskwise certificate of
[[thm-complex-resolvent-cover-certificate-soundness]]. A scalar disk error
alone does not give this matrix bound for a nonnormal matrix.

If the validator's input has $n\ge1$ and [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] returns `certified-resolvent-cover` with bound $m$, then every $A$ in the input family and every $z$ on the supplied contour segments satisfy that $zI-A$ is invertible and $\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le m$. The result does not count eigenvalues inside the contour.

Let $\|\cdot\|$ be a submultiplicative norm on square matrices. Suppose
$X_{j+1}=X_j^2$ and $\widehat X_{j+1}=\widehat X_j^2+E_j$ for matrices of the
same size. If $e_j=\|\widehat X_j-X_j\|$, then
$$e_{j+1}\le\bigl(2\|X_j\|+e_j\bigr)e_j+\|E_j\|.$$
The term $E_j$ records the entire defect in the computed squaring.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, define
$$
\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\sum_{j=1}^n |a_{ij}|.
$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$, define $\|x\|_\infty:=\max_j|x_j|$. The absolute value is the complex modulus $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$. The subscript on the matrix norm emphasizes that entries and vectors are complex; this definition is not an appeal to the real-only induced matrix p-norm convention. For square matrices the identity has norm $1$.

Use $\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ and $\|x\|_\infty$ from [[def-complex-infinity-matrix-norm]]. For compatible complex matrices and vectors with every row and column dimension positive,
$$\|Ax\|_\infty\le\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\|x\|_\infty,\qquad \|AB\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on an
open set $\Omega$ containing $\sigma(A)$. The Jordan expression in
[[def-analytic-primary-matrix-function]] is independent of the chosen Jordan
representation and satisfies $f(XAX^{-1})=Xf(A)X^{-1}$ for every invertible
$X$. It equals $p(A)$ for the unique Hermite polynomial $p$ matching the
derivatives of $f$ at the Jordan eigenvalue data; in particular, it commutes
with $A$. For holomorphic $f,g$ on $\Omega$, it also satisfies
$(fg)(A)=f(A)g(A)$. If $A$ is normal, it equals the spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]].

If $T$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks $T_{ii}$ and $f$ is
holomorphic on a neighborhood of $\sigma(T)$, then $f(T)$ is block upper
triangular and its diagonal blocks are $f(T_{ii})$.

For the contour formula, let $\Gamma$ be a finite complex cycle with trace in
$\Omega$, null-homologous in $\Omega$, disjoint from $\sigma(A)$, and with
index $n(\Gamma,\lambda)=1$ for every $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$. Then, with the
matrix line integral taken entry by entry,
$$f(A)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f(z)(zI-A)^{-1}\,dz.$$

For an integer $m\ge0$, put
$$a_{m,j}:=\frac{(2m-j)!\,m!}{(2m)!\,j!\,(m-j)!}\qquad(0\le j\le m), \qquad p_m(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m a_{m,j}z^j, \qquad q_m(z):=p_m(-z).$$
The diagonal Padé rational function of order $m$ for the scalar exponential
[[def-complex-exponential]] is
$$r_m(z):=\frac{p_m(z)}{q_m(z)}$$
at every $z\in\mathbb C$ for which $q_m(z)\ne0$. The pair is normalized by
$p_m(0)=q_m(0)=1$. This definition does not assign a value at a zero of the
denominator.

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ whose stored entries
are representable in the operationwise model, a Padé order $m\ge0$, an integer
scaling count $s\ge0$, finite nonnegative integer Householder-candidate and squaring-operation budgets,
finite scalar-series budgets, and an
error policy that is either candidate-only or certify. The procedure never
selects adaptive Higham parameters. Certification data, including contour
vertices and the radius, have exact dyadic or rational encodings.

1. Interpret the stored entries of $A$ as their exact real/imaginary values and
   form $B=2^{-s}A$ exactly. Evaluate $P=p_m(B)$ and $Q=q_m(B)$ by exact
   controller matrix arithmetic: increasing-index sums/products and finite
   polynomial powers with their rational coefficients. Use the exact real-RAM
   controller declared in [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]];
   the optional rational adapter is used only when all required actual
   encodings are supplied. No dyadic representation is assumed for the
   abstract floating model.
2. Call [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]] on $QX=P$, explicitly passing the supplied finite Householder-candidate operation budget $K_H$. Continue only if the returned record contains a complete finite stored $n\times n$ matrix, with all entries marked complete, and status `verified-solution` or `candidate-unverified`. A partial candidate or any budget, range, representation or other failure is propagated with its original status and available partial record; do not square it. Retain a complete unverified candidate only in candidate-only mode; certification mode returns denominator-unverified. A complete matrix accompanying a failure status does not authorize continuation.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,s-1$, compute the next matrix square in the operationwise
   model. A range failure returns range-failure with the last candidate.
   Retain their exact stored real values and form
   $D_j=\widehat X_{j+1}-\widehat X_j^2$ by the exact controller's finite
   matrix loops. Set
   $\delta_j=\max_i\sum_k(|\operatorname{Re}(D_j)_{ik}|
   +|\operatorname{Im}(D_j)_{ik}|)$; this exact nonnegative real number bounds
   $\|D_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$.
4. In candidate-only mode, return the final candidate with status
   unevaluated-error-bound. Certification mode has these caller preconditions,
   which the procedure does not itself verify: (a) a supplied polygonal Cauchy
   cycle $\Gamma$ with dyadic vertices, trace in a disk $|z|\le\rho$ for
   dyadic $\rho>0$, $\sigma(B)\subset\{|z|<\rho\}$, disjointness from
   $\sigma(B)$, index one on $\sigma(B)$, and null-homology in that disk;
   (b) $d_m(\rho)>0$; (c) a supplied finite dyadic resolvent-cover input for
   the singleton family $\{B\}$; and (d) a finite term budget $K$.
   The contour-validator call
   [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] must return
   certified-resolvent-cover with bound $M$, or the procedure returns
   inconclusive-resolvent. The validator checks resolvent inequalities and
   segment coverage only; it does not validate the caller's topological
   preconditions or count enclosed eigenvalues. Here $\sigma(B)$ denotes the
   eigenvalue set of $B$ from
   [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]].
5. For $x=\rho$ and for
   $\alpha=\max_i\sum_j(|\operatorname{Re}A_{ij}|+
   |\operatorname{Im}A_{ij}|)$, compute an upper bound $U(x)$ for $e^x$ as
   follows. If $x=0$, set $U(x)=1$. Otherwise, if $x\ge K+2$, return
   inconclusive-scalar-tail. If $x<K+2$, put
   $r=x/(K+2)$,
   $U(x)=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!+
   [x^{K+1}/(K+1)!]/(1-r)$.
   The scalar-tail inequality used by the error theorem is proved separately there; this step defines the finite expression, rather than treating a Definition sentence as its proof.
6. Write the supplied finite polygonal chain as $\Gamma=\sum_\nu m_\nu\gamma_\nu$, with integer coefficients. Let $\ell=\sum_\nu |m_\nu|\sum_{e\text{ in }\gamma_\nu}(|\Delta\operatorname{Re}e|+|\Delta\operatorname{Im}e|)$; then
   $\ell$ is an exact rational upper bound for the coefficient-weighted contour length $L_\Gamma=\sum_\nu|m_\nu|L(\gamma_\nu)$ (the supplied vertices have rational/dyadic encodings). Put
   $\epsilon=\rho^{2m+1}U(\rho)(m!)^2/
   ((2m)!(2m+1)!d_m(\rho))$. Since
   $\pi/4=\int_0^1(1+x^2)^{-1}\,dx$, the finite identity
   $1/(1+x^2)=\sum_{k=0}^7(-1)^kx^{2k}+x^{16}/(1+x^2)$ on $[0,1]$ gives
   $\pi/4>33976/45045>3/4$, hence $1/(2\pi)<1/6$. Set
   $E_0=\ell\epsilon M/6$.
7. For each squaring use
   $E_{j+1}=(2U(\alpha)+E_j)E_j+\delta_j$.
   If every computed certification check succeeded, the denominator solve
   returned verified-solution, and the caller preconditions hold, return the
   final candidate with status conditional-error-bound and bound $E_s$.
   Otherwise retain the candidate and return
   the corresponding inconclusive status.

The exact controller uses only prescribed finite field-expression trees and
loops over dimensions, $m,s$ and the finite scalar-series term budget $K$;
absolute values/maxima use exact comparisons. It performs no additional
unprovided certification call. Count every rounded real primitive of a square
in row-major/increasing inner-index order against an explicitly supplied
finite squaring-operation budget, and propagate `budget-exhausted` before an
unaffordable operation. The solve uses its separately supplied finite
candidate-operation budget. Exact controller work is separate: its values
need not be rational, and no bit-computability or total bit-cost bound for
arbitrary real encodings is claimed. For the optional rational adapter with
all values encoded, these same finite formulas use exact rational arithmetic.
All loops are finite. The conditional-error-bound status is sound
only under the caller preconditions in step 4 and does not mean that the
procedure checked contour topology or eigenvalue count. No floating-point
stability is asserted for the candidate alone.

derivations.claim: For $x=0$ the series gives $e^0=1=U(0)$. For $0<x<K+2$, put $a_j=x^j/j!$ and $r=x/(K+2)<1$. For every $j\ge K+1$, $a_{j+1}/a_j=x/(j+1)\le r$. Induction yields $a_{K+1+q}\le a_{K+1}r^q$. Finite geometric sums and passage to the convergent series give $\sum_{j=K+1}^\infty a_j\le a_{K+1}/(1-r)$. Adding the first $K+1$ terms proves $e^x\le U(x)$ for both actual scalar inputs. This uses the explicit exponential series in [F3], not an unproved algorithm property.

Integrating [L1] gives a positive remainder and the partial sum $1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\frac19-\frac1{11}+\frac1{13}-\frac1{15}=(45045-15015+9009-6435+5005-4095+3465-3003)/45045=33976/45045$. Since $4\cdot33976=135904>135135=3\cdot45045$, we have $\pi/4>3/4$, hence $\pi>3$ and $1/(2\pi)<1/6$. Therefore $L_\Gamma\varepsilon M/(2\pi)\le\ell\varepsilon M/6$ whenever $L_\Gamma\le\ell$.

Let $B=2^{-s}A$. Since $d_m(\rho)>0$, [F3] makes $q_m$ nonzero throughout $|z|\le\rho$, which contains $\sigma(B)$ by the caller's topological hypothesis. In a Jordan basis of $B$, polynomial evaluation makes each block of $Q_m(B)$ upper triangular with diagonal $q_m(\lambda)$, so $Q_m(B)$ is invertible. The polynomial $q_m$ has finitely many zeros and none in the closed disk by [F3]; hence some $\eta>0$ makes $q_m$ nonzero on the open disk $D(0,\rho+\eta)$, which contains both $\Gamma$ and $\sigma(B)$. Thus $1/q_m$ is holomorphic there. By the product rule [F9] applied to $q_m(1/q_m)=1$, $Q_m(B)(1/q_m)(B)=I$, hence $(1/q_m)(B)=Q_m(B)^{-1}$. Applying [F9] again to $r_m=p_m(1/q_m)$ from [F10] gives $r_m(B)=P_m(B)Q_m(B)^{-1}$. The polynomial matrices $P_m(B)$ and $Q_m(B)$ commute, so this is also $Q_m(B)^{-1}P_m(B)$. The exact solve from [F2] therefore makes the initial candidate $X_0=r_m(B)$.

Put $X_j=\exp(2^jB)$ for $0\le j\le s$. The exponential semigroup law in [F8] gives $X_{j+1}=X_j^2$ and $X_s=\exp(A)$. The row-sum matrix norm is the operator norm induced by the vector infinity norm: the row triangle inequality gives the upper bound, and for a maximizing row choose each nonzero coordinate of $x$ to cancel the phase of that matrix entry, with arbitrary unit phases for zero entries; then $\|x\|_\infty=1$ and that row attains its row sum. By [F7] and [F8], $\|X_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le e^{2^j\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}}\le e^\alpha\le U(\alpha)$ by [F11], where $\alpha\ge\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ is the exact row bound used by the algorithm.

The scalar bound [F3] applies at every point of $\Gamma$ because its trace lies in $|z|\le\rho$. Since $e^\rho\le U(\rho)$ by [F11], it gives $\sup_{\Gamma}|e^z-r_m(z)|\le\varepsilon$ with the $\varepsilon$ computed by the algorithm. The validator gives the resolvent bound $M$ by [F5]; applying [F4] and then step 1.2 gives $\|X_0-e^B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \frac{L_\Gamma}{2\pi}\varepsilon M\le\frac{\ell\varepsilon M}{6}=E_0.$

For each returned square, the exact controller audit defines $D_j=\widehat X_{j+1}-\widehat X_j^2$. Since $|x+iy|\le|x|+|y|$, its row sums give $\|D_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le\delta_j$. If $\|\widehat X_j-X_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le E_j$, [F6] and step 2.1 imply $\|\widehat X_{j+1}-X_{j+1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le(2U(\alpha)+E_j)E_j+\delta_j=E_{j+1}.$ Starting from step 2.2, induction proves this bound for every $j\le s$.
At $j=s$, $X_s=\exp(A)$ by step 2.1, so step 3.1 gives $\|\widehat X_s-\exp(A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le E_s$, as claimed.

If [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]] returns
verified-solution with output $X$ for exact complex matrices $M,C$ in its declared exact-controller model, then
$MX=C$ exactly. If $M$ is invertible, this solution is unique; in particular,
when used with an invertible Padé denominator, it is the exact denominator solve. This includes the original rational-input
instance and its finite exact rational audit whenever the adapter encodings
are supplied.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For $m\ge0$ and $\rho\ge0$, put
$$d_m(\rho):=1-\sum_{j=1}^m a_{m,j}\rho^j,$$
with the empty sum equal to zero and $a_{m,j}$ as in
[[def-diagonal-pade-approximant-for-exponential]]. If $d_m(\rho)>0$, then
$q_m$ has no zero in $|z|\le\rho$ and, for every such $z$,
$$\left|e^z-r_m(z)\right| \le \frac{\rho^{2m+1}e^\rho(m!)^2} {(2m)!(2m+1)!\,d_m(\rho)}.$$
This is a finite-order bound; it makes no adaptive choice of $m$ or scaling.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $f$ be holomorphic on an open
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ containing $\sigma(A)$, and let $r$ be rational
with no pole on $\Omega$. Let $\Gamma$ be an admissible Cauchy cycle for $A$
contained in $\Omega$, with total contour length $L_\Gamma$. Suppose
$$\sup_{z\in\Gamma}|f(z)-r(z)|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \sup_{z\in\Gamma}\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le M.$$
Then
$$\|f(A)-r(A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le \frac{L_\Gamma}{2\pi}\,\varepsilon M.$$
The resolvent hypothesis may be supplied by the diskwise certificate of
[[thm-complex-resolvent-cover-certificate-soundness]]. A scalar disk error
alone does not give this matrix bound for a nonnormal matrix.

If the validator's input has $n\ge1$ and [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] returns `certified-resolvent-cover` with bound $m$, then every $A$ in the input family and every $z$ on the supplied contour segments satisfy that $zI-A$ is invertible and $\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le m$. The result does not count eigenvalues inside the contour.

Let $\|\cdot\|$ be a submultiplicative norm on square matrices. Suppose
$X_{j+1}=X_j^2$ and $\widehat X_{j+1}=\widehat X_j^2+E_j$ for matrices of the
same size. If $e_j=\|\widehat X_j-X_j\|$, then
$$e_{j+1}\le\bigl(2\|X_j\|+e_j\bigr)e_j+\|E_j\|.$$
The term $E_j$ records the entire defect in the computed squaring.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, define
$$
\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\sum_{j=1}^n |a_{ij}|.
$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$, define $\|x\|_\infty:=\max_j|x_j|$. The absolute value is the complex modulus $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$. The subscript on the matrix norm emphasizes that entries and vectors are complex; this definition is not an appeal to the real-only induced matrix p-norm convention. For square matrices the identity has norm $1$.

Use $\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ and $\|x\|_\infty$ from [[def-complex-infinity-matrix-norm]]. For compatible complex matrices and vectors with every row and column dimension positive,
$$\|Ax\|_\infty\le\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\|x\|_\infty,\qquad \|AB\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on an
open set $\Omega$ containing $\sigma(A)$. The Jordan expression in
[[def-analytic-primary-matrix-function]] is independent of the chosen Jordan
representation and satisfies $f(XAX^{-1})=Xf(A)X^{-1}$ for every invertible
$X$. It equals $p(A)$ for the unique Hermite polynomial $p$ matching the
derivatives of $f$ at the Jordan eigenvalue data; in particular, it commutes
with $A$. For holomorphic $f,g$ on $\Omega$, it also satisfies
$(fg)(A)=f(A)g(A)$. If $A$ is normal, it equals the spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]].

If $T$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks $T_{ii}$ and $f$ is
holomorphic on a neighborhood of $\sigma(T)$, then $f(T)$ is block upper
triangular and its diagonal blocks are $f(T_{ii})$.

For the contour formula, let $\Gamma$ be a finite complex cycle with trace in
$\Omega$, null-homologous in $\Omega$, disjoint from $\sigma(A)$, and with
index $n(\Gamma,\lambda)=1$ for every $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$. Then, with the
matrix line integral taken entry by entry,
$$f(A)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f(z)(zI-A)^{-1}\,dz.$$

For an integer $m\ge0$, put

[[def-complex-exponential]] is
$$r_m(z):=\frac{p_m(z)}{q_m(z)}$$
at every $z\in\mathbb C$ for which $q_m(z)\ne0$. The pair is normalized by

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ whose stored entries
are representable in the operationwise model, a Padé order $m\ge0$, an integer
scaling count $s\ge0$, finite nonnegative integer Householder-candidate and squaring-operation budgets,
finite scalar-series budgets, and an
error policy that is either candidate-only or certify. The procedure never
selects adaptive Higham parameters. Certification data, including contour
vertices and the radius, have exact dyadic or rational encodings.

1. Interpret the stored entries of $A$ as their exact real/imaginary values and

   polynomial powers with their rational coefficients. Use the exact real-RAM
   controller declared in [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]];
   the optional rational adapter is used only when all required actual
   encodings are supplied. No dyadic representation is assumed for the
   abstract floating model.
2. Call [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]] on $QX=P$. If it
   returns a candidate, retain that candidate. If it returns a failure without
   a candidate, propagate its status. If the solve is not verified, continue
   only in candidate-only mode; certification mode returns
   denominator-unverified.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,s-1$, compute the next matrix square in the operationwise
   model. A range failure returns range-failure with the last candidate.
   Retain their exact stored real values and form
   $D_j=\widehat X_{j+1}-\widehat X_j^2$ by the exact controller's finite
   matrix loops. Set
   $\delta_j=\max_i\sum_k(|\operatorname{Re}(D_j)_{ik}|
   +|\operatorname{Im}(D_j)_{ik}|)$; this exact nonnegative real number bounds
   $\|D_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$.
4. In candidate-only mode, return the final candidate with status
   unevaluated-error-bound. Certification mode has these caller preconditions,
   which the procedure does not itself verify: (a) a supplied polygonal Cauchy
   cycle $\Gamma$ with dyadic vertices, trace in a disk $|z|\le\rho$ for
   dyadic $\rho>0$, $\sigma(B)\subset\{|z|<\rho\}$, disjointness from
   $\sigma(B)$, index one on $\sigma(B)$, and null-homology in that disk;
   (b) $d_m(\rho)>0$; (c) a supplied finite dyadic resolvent-cover input for
   the singleton family $\{B\}$; and (d) a finite term budget $K$.
   The contour-validator call
   [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] must return
   certified-resolvent-cover with bound $M$, or the procedure returns
   inconclusive-resolvent. The validator checks resolvent inequalities and
   segment coverage only; it does not validate the caller's topological
   preconditions or count enclosed eigenvalues. Here $\sigma(B)$ denotes the
   eigenvalue set of $B$ from
   [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]].

   $\alpha=\max_i\sum_j(|\operatorname{Re}A_{ij}|+

   inconclusive-scalar-tail. If $x<K+2$, put
   $r=x/(K+2)$,
   $U(x)=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!+
   [x^{K+1}/(K+1)!]/(1-r)$.
   The geometric tail bound makes $U(x)\ge e^x$.

   $|\Delta\operatorname{Re}z|+|\Delta\operatorname{Im}z|$; then
   $\ell$ is an exact rational upper bound for the contour length (the supplied vertices have rational/dyadic encodings). Put
   $\epsilon=\rho^{2m+1}U(\rho)(m!)^2/
   ((2m)!(2m+1)!d_m(\rho))$. Since

   returned verified-solution, and the caller preconditions hold, return the
   final candidate with status conditional-error-bound and bound $E_s$.

derivations.claim: Integrating [L1] gives a positive remainder and the partial sum $1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\frac19-\frac1{11}+\frac1{13}-\frac1{15}=(45045-15015+9009-6435+5005-4095+3465-3003)/45045=33976/45045$. Since $4\cdot33976=135904>135135=3\cdot45045$, we have $\pi/4>3/4$, hence $\pi>3$ and $1/(2\pi)<1/6$. Therefore $L_\Gamma\varepsilon M/(2\pi)\le\ell\varepsilon M/6$ whenever $L_\Gamma\le\ell$.

Let $B=2^{-s}A$. Since $d_m(\rho)>0$, [F3] makes $q_m$ nonzero throughout $|z|\le\rho$, which contains $\sigma(B)$ by the caller's topological hypothesis. In a Jordan basis of $B$, polynomial evaluation makes each block of $Q_m(B)$ upper triangular with diagonal $q_m(\lambda)$, so $Q_m(B)$ is invertible. The polynomial $q_m$ has finitely many zeros and none in the closed disk by [F3]; hence some $\eta>0$ makes $q_m$ nonzero on the open disk $D(0,\rho+\eta)$, which contains both $\Gamma$ and $\sigma(B)$. Thus $1/q_m$ is holomorphic there. By the product rule [F9] applied to $q_m(1/q_m)=1$, $Q_m(B)(1/q_m)(B)=I$, hence $(1/q_m)(B)=Q_m(B)^{-1}$. Applying [F9] again to $r_m=p_m(1/q_m)$ from [F10] gives $r_m(B)=P_m(B)Q_m(B)^{-1}$. The polynomial matrices $P_m(B)$ and $Q_m(B)$ commute, so this is also $Q_m(B)^{-1}P_m(B)$. The exact solve from [F2] therefore makes the initial candidate $X_0=r_m(B)$.

Put $X_j=\exp(2^jB)$ for $0\le j\le s$. The exponential semigroup law in [F8] gives $X_{j+1}=X_j^2$ and $X_s=\exp(A)$. The row-sum matrix norm is the operator norm induced by the vector infinity norm: the row triangle inequality gives the upper bound, and for a maximizing row choose each nonzero coordinate of $x$ to cancel the phase of that matrix entry, with arbitrary unit phases for zero entries; then $\|x\|_\infty=1$ and that row attains its row sum. By [F7] and [F8], $\|X_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le e^{2^j\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}}\le e^\alpha\le U(\alpha)$ by [F11], where $\alpha\ge\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ is the exact row bound used by the algorithm.

The scalar bound [F3] applies at every point of $\Gamma$ because its trace lies in $|z|\le\rho$. Since $e^\rho\le U(\rho)$ by [F11], it gives $\sup_{\Gamma}|e^z-r_m(z)|\le\varepsilon$ with the $\varepsilon$ computed by the algorithm. The validator gives the resolvent bound $M$ by [F5]; applying [F4] and then step 1.1 gives $\|X_0-e^B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \frac{L_\Gamma}{2\pi}\varepsilon M\le\frac{\ell\varepsilon M}{6}=E_0.$

For each returned square, the exact controller audit defines $D_j=\widehat X_{j+1}-\widehat X_j^2$. Since $|x+iy|\le|x|+|y|$, its row sums give $\|D_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le\delta_j$. If $\|\widehat X_j-X_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le E_j$, [F6] and step 1.3 imply $\|\widehat X_{j+1}-X_{j+1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le(2U(\alpha)+E_j)E_j+\delta_j=E_{j+1}.$ Starting from step 2.1, induction proves this bound for every $j\le s$.
At $j=s$, $X_s=\exp(A)$ by step 1.3, so step 3.1 gives $\|\widehat X_s-\exp(A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le E_s$, as claimed.

If this holds at $k$, then $X_k^{-*}=U g_k(H)^{-1}$ because $U^*U=I$ and $g_k(H)$ is positive diagonal; substituting into [F3] proves the next formula and shows every iterate is invertible.

For each scalar $\sigma_i>0$, $g_1(\sigma_i)-1=(\sigma_i-1)^2/(2\sigma_i)\ge0$, so $g_1(\sigma_i)\ge1$. If $y\ge1$, then $\frac12(y+y^{-1})\le y$, and $\frac12(y+y^{-1})-1=(y-1)^2/(2y)$. Hence each sequence $g_k(\sigma_i)$ for $k\ge1$ decreases to a limit $y\ge1$ satisfying $y=(y+y^{-1})/2$, so $y=1$. The displayed identity also gives $|g_{k+1}(\sigma_i)-1|\le |g_k(\sigma_i)-1|^2/2$ for $k\ge1$.
Since $U$ is unitary and $g_k(H)$ is diagonal, $\|X_k-U\|_2=\max_i|g_k(\sigma_i)-1|$. Taking maxima in step 2.1 proves $X_k\to U$ and the stated quadratic bound.

derivations.claim: In a Jordan representation of $A$, [F1]–[F2] give $S=I$ on every right-half-plane block and $S=-I$ on every left-half-plane block. Hence $S^2=I$ and $AS=SA$. Conjugate the exact iterates into this basis. Initially they are block diagonal with upper-triangular Jordan blocks. If $X_k$ has this form, its inverse, when defined, has the same block structure and its diagonal entries are the reciprocals of those of $X_k$. Thus each diagonal entry follows the scalar update $\lambda_{k+1}=(\lambda_k+\lambda_k^{-1})/2$. Whenever $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_k\ne0$, $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_{k+1} =\frac{\operatorname{Re}\lambda_k}{2} \left(1+|\lambda_k|^{-2}\right),$ so its nonzero real-part sign is unchanged. By induction all diagonal entries remain nonzero and off $i\mathbb R$, each $X_k$ is invertible, and the next update is defined.

Since the Jordan-block diagonal values remain in the same half-planes, [F2] gives $\operatorname{sign}(X_k)=S$ for every $k$. Also $X_k$ commutes with $S$: this holds for $X_0=A$, and if it holds for $X_k$, then its inverse also commutes with $S$, so the update [F3] preserves commutation. The eigenvalues of $X_k+S$ are $\lambda_k+s$ on the corresponding blocks, with $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_k+s)\ne0$ because $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_k$ has sign $s$. Thus $X_k+S$ is invertible. Define $G_k=(X_k-S)(X_k+S)^{-1}$.

Using $S^2=I$ and commutation with $X_k$, expansion gives $X_{k+1}\pm S=\frac12X_k^{-1}(X_k\pm S)^2, \qquad G_{k+1}=G_k^2.$ Hence $G_k=G_0^{2^k}$. The eigenvalues of $G_0$ are $(\lambda-s)/(\lambda+s)$; their moduli are less than one because $|\lambda+s|^2-|\lambda-s|^2=4s\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0$.

In a Jordan basis of $A$, $G_0=(A-S)(A+S)^{-1}$ is block upper triangular; on a block at $\lambda$ its diagonal is $\mu=(\lambda-s)/(\lambda+s)$ and its strictly upper triangular part is nilpotent, say $N_0^d=0$. Its $q$th power is $\sum_{j<d}\binom qj\mu^{q-j}N_0^j$. Each term tends to zero as $q\to\infty$ because $|\mu|<1$ and exponential decay dominates the polynomial factor $\binom qj$; if $\mu=0$, the nilpotent block power is eventually zero. Thus $G_0^{2^k}\to0$. The eigenvalues of $G_k=G_0^{2^k}$ have modulus less than one, so $I-G_k$ is invertible. Rearranging the definition of $G_k$ gives $X_k=(I-G_k)^{-1}(I+G_k)S$, so $X_k\to S$.

Direct expansion, using $X_kS=SX_k$ and $S^2=I$, gives $X_{k+1}-S=\frac12X_k^{-1}(X_k-S)^2$. Taking any submultiplicative norm proves the stated quadratic inequality. To bound the inverse near the limit, write $X_k=S(I+Y_k)$ with $Y_k=S^{-1}(X_k-S)$. Since $X_k\to S$, eventually $\|Y_k\|<1/2$. The geometric series $\sum_{j\ge0}(-Y_k)^j$ is Cauchy in the chosen norm because its tail is bounded by the scalar geometric tail; the matrix space is complete by [F4]. Multiplication of its partial sums by $I+Y_k$ shows its sum is $(I+Y_k)^{-1}$, whose norm is at most $\|I\|+\|Y_k\|/(1-\|Y_k\|)\le\|I\|+1$. Thus $\|X_k^{-1}\|\le(\|I\|+1)\|S^{-1}\|$ eventually, so the displayed inequality has a fixed quadratic constant near the limit.

1. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form with Householder similarities. For $k=1,\ldots,\max(n-2,0)$ in increasing order, use active indices $S=\{k+1,\ldots,n\}$, target $x=H_{S,k}$, and trailing left panel $B=H_{S,\{k+1,\ldots,n\}}$ with columns in increasing order. In the real branch use [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] for the finite left application and overwrite; in the complex branch use [[alg-complex-scaled-householder-reflector-step]]. Complete each similarity by the right application above on columns $S$. If the resulting matrix fails the exact upper-Hessenberg zero-pattern check, return bulge-chase-invariant-failure with the partial factors. Store the exact unitary reflector factors as a product representation $Q_0$.
2. At each sweep, test every active first-subdiagonal entry by
   $$|h_{i,i-1}|\le\tau\bigl(|h_{i-1,i-1}|+|h_{i,i}|\bigr).$$
   For a complex entry $z=a+ib$, evaluate $|z|$ by $s=\max(|a|,|b|)$ and $s\sqrt{(a/s)^2+(b/s)^2}$ when $z\ne0$, with divisions, squares, sum, square root and final scaling rounded in the stated order; use $|0|=0$. Return range-failure if this evaluation fails. Compute the diagonal-magnitude sum first, then multiply by $\tau$ in the operationwise model; compare the resulting finite values exactly. When the test holds, set that entry to zero, record its original value as a deflation perturbation, and split the active block. The equality case deflates. Do not use the Hermitian-tridiagonal Wilkinson shift rule for a general Hessenberg matrix.
3. Check for the target Schur block structure after initialization and after each sweep. A complex active block of size at least two uses a single shift, normally its bottom-right entry. A real active block of size at least two uses the real quadratic $p(z)=z^2-sz+t$ with trailing block $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$; compute $s=\operatorname{fl}(a+d)$ and $t=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ad)-\operatorname{fl}(bc))$ in that order, returning range-failure if an operation fails. Maintain a counter for each active block, reset it after any deflation in that block, and after $h$ consecutive sweeps without deflation consume that block's next declared exceptional shift or real quadratic. If the required table entry is absent, return stagnation-exhausted.
4. Apply the corresponding implicit bulge chase from [[alg-exact-francis-hessenberg-qr-step]]. For the initial single-shift vector compute $x_1=\operatorname{fl}(h_{11}-\mu)$ and $x_i=h_{i1}$ for $i>1$. For the initial real double-shift vector, compute $u=He_1$, then $w=Hu$ by left-to-right rounded matrix-vector products, then $x=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(w-su)+te_1)$ componentwise. Compute only the first $r+1$ components from the Hessenberg support pattern; on range failure return the operation index and partial factors. For a chase at column $j$, use active indices $S=I_j$, target $x=H_{S,j}$, and trailing left panel $B=H_{S,\{j+1,\ldots,n\}}$ with columns in increasing order. Call the real or complex formation routine, write the target tail zeros exactly, complete the two-sided update by the right-kernel order above on columns $S$, and append the exact reflector representation to $Q$. In the initial polynomial-vector step there is no matrix-target column; use the full active row panel for the left update and then apply the right update to its active columns. If the exact routine or its finite-precision realization returns bulge-chase-invariant-failure, return that status with the partial matrix and factors. Use [[lem-two-sided-scaled-householder-similarity-error]] to store the proved two-sided coefficient $\alpha_{m_j}=a_{m_j}+b_{m_j}+a_{m_j}b_{m_j}$, with $a$ the target-overwrite coefficient or separate-block coefficient as actually used and $b$ the right separate-block coefficient. This gives $\|E_j\|_F\le\alpha_{m_j}\|\widehat H_{j-1}\|_F$ when its $m_ju<1$ and range hypotheses hold. Apply the same certificate to every Hessenberg-initialization similarity. If any step lacks that certificate, retain the residual diagnostic and set the backward-error-certificate status to inconclusive.
5. Stop with Schur-computed when every complex block has size one, or every real block has size one or is a $2\times2$ block with negative characteristic-polynomial discriminant. Use the supplied evaluator, or the finite integer recipe in [[lem-exact-rational-two-by-two-discriminant-sign]] when exact rational/dyadic encodings are available, for each real block's $\operatorname{discSign}$ as defined in [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]]. If no exact sign is available, return schur-type-undecided and do not claim Schur-computed. If the target check fails when the sweep count reaches $N$, return budget-exhausted; in particular, with $N=0$ return Schur-computed only when the initialized matrix already has the target block structure. Return the partial matrix and factors on every failure or nonconvergence status.

For $z\ne0$ with principal polar form $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$, define the **principal logarithm**
$$\operatorname{Log}z:=\log r+i\theta.$$
The set of all complex logarithms of $z$ is
$$\log_{\mathrm{multi}}z:=\{v\in\mathbb C:\exp v=z\}.$$
For $w\in\mathbb C$, define the **principal power** and the **multivalued power** respectively by
$$z^w_{\mathrm{pr}}:=\exp(w\operatorname{Log}z),\qquad z^w_{\mathrm{multi}}:=\{\exp(wv):v\in\log_{\mathrm{multi}}z\}.$$
Thus the first is one specified complex number and the second is a set of complex numbers; neither notation silently identifies them. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.
